author: Eirik Stonetongue, Keeper of the Barrow Records
pages:
#Before the Kings

There was a time, the oldest songs say, when the north had no kings at all, only masters. The masters had wings, and scales like overlapping shields, and voices that could split a mountain. They were the dragons, and men were their servants.

#The Dragon Priests

The dragons did not rule alone. They chose mortal priests to govern in their name, and rewarded them with long life and terrible power. The priests built temples on the high peaks and buried themselves, when death finally came, in great barrows guarded by their loyal dead.

Many of those barrows still stand. Many of those guardians still keep watch. The draugr you meet in the old tombs are not mindless; they are obedient, and their orders have simply never been cancelled.

#The Rebellion

No empire of fear lasts forever. The songs say that a few dragons took pity on mortals, or perhaps simply grew bored of their brothers, and taught a handful of men the secret of the Voice: how to speak in the dragons' own tongue and bend the world with words.

Armed with the Voice, the rebels made war on their masters. The war shook the mountains for generations. When it ended, the dragons were gone from the sky, and the priests were sealed in their tombs.

#Gone, But Not Dead

Here the songs disagree. Some say every dragon was slain. Others say the dragons merely slept, or hid, or were scattered beyond the edges of the world, and that one day they will return.

I have read both kinds of song. I note only that the songs which say the dragons are gone forever are always the newer ones.
